blocks.text: On a winter morning in a village, or at a wedding in Ashgabat, you will see men in a *telpek*: a tall, shaggy hat of sheepskin, white, black or brown. It is the best-known piece of Turkmen dress, and many Turkmens see it as a sign of who they are.

**How a telpek is made.** It is a soft leather cap covered with sheepskin, wool side out. Preparing the skin takes weeks: it is salted for several days, softened with sour milk, left to age, then scraped smooth with a stone, often by several members of one family. The thick wool keeps out both the winter cold and the summer heat. Younger men tend to wear white telpeks, older men grey or black ones, and under the telpek a man wears a small skullcap, so that his head is never bare.

**Men's dress.** Until the 1920s a Turkmen man wore loose white trousers, a shirt and a sash, and over them a long silk robe with tight sleeves, the *don*. According to the Encyclopaedia Iranica, younger men wore a red robe, while men over forty wore one with an extra white stripe, so that the robe showed a man's age.

**Women's dress.** The main garment is the *köýnek*, a long, straight dress, once of silk and often deep red, with embroidery around the neck and the cuffs. Under it women wore trousers whose embroidered cuffs showed at the ankle. Girls wore a small embroidered cap, the *tahýa*; married women wore a headband and a headscarf, so that dress and colour told people a woman's age and status. On formal occasions, Teke women draped a mantle over a tall headdress: the *çyrpy*, with tiny false sleeves, or the *kürte*, with full ones.

**Silver.** A festive Turkmen outfit is not complete without silver: bracelets, pendants and collars, heart-shaped pendants on the braids, and tall headdresses covered with silver plates, which among the Teke are often gilded and set with red carnelian. Some pieces held amulets. The styles differ from tribe to tribe, like the *göl* of the carpets ([A2 unit 4](a2-u04-culture)).

**Today.** In the towns many people dress as people do anywhere, but long embroidered dresses are still common in Ashgabat, and the telpek comes out for holidays, weddings and official occasions. In the countryside, away from the big towns, it is still part of everyday dress.

blocks.text: *türkmen telpegi*, a Turkmen telpek, is a compound; *gyşky telpek* is a winter one; and to ask who it belongs to, *Bu telpek kimiňki?*
With this unit's grammar, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Bu türkmen telpegi atamyňky. Ol gara telpek, ak däl. Atam ony gyşda hem, tomusda hem geýýär. Telpegiň aşagyndaky tahýa hem onuňky. Toýdaky aýallaryň köýnekleri uzyn we gyzyl.
blocks.en: This Turkmen telpek is my grandfather's. It's a black telpek, not a white one. My grandfather wears it in winter and in summer. The skullcap under the telpek is his too. The dresses of the women at the wedding are long and red.

questions.q: What is a telpek made of?
questions.explain: A leather cap covered with sheepskin, wool side out.

questions.q: According to the Encyclopaedia Iranica, how did a man's robe show that he was over forty?

sources.title: Telpek
sources.note: A leather cap covered with sheepskin, white, black or dark brown; weeks of work, salting, softening with sour milk or kefir, ageing, scraping with a stone, often by family members; insulation against extreme temperatures; worn on official occasions and popular in rural areas; younger men white, older grey or black; seen as a symbol of Turkmen identity

sources.title: Clothing xxvi. Clothing and jewelry of the Turkmen
sources.note: Men's dress before the 1920s (silk robe, white trousers, shirt, sash, telpek over a skullcap); red robes for young men, an extra white stripe after forty; the köýnek with embroidered neck and cuffs, embroidered trouser cuffs; girls' skullcaps, married women's headband and headcloth; the Teke çyrpy and the full-sleeved kürte; silver plaques, gilt and carnelian among the Teke, pendants, collars, amulets; differences by tribe
